title: Narada's monkey face
hookLine: proud Narada asks for Vishnu's handsome face and gets a monkey's; why the arti flame burns camphor, and the ego with it
last: SANDHYA — PRAY WHERE THE DAY JOINS.

cards: Narada, the wandering sage with the veena, once sat in such deep meditation that Kama, the god of desire, was sent to distract him, and failed. Narada was thrilled. I've beaten desire, he thought.
Me. He told Shiva, who said kindly: wonderful, but don't go telling Vishnu. He told Vishnu.

So Vishnu let him wander into a beautiful city where a princess was choosing a husband. Narada fell for her on the spot and begged Vishnu: give me your face, so she'll pick me. Vishnu said: I'll do what's best for you.
Narada swept into the hall, sure he looked like Vishnu. He had the face of a monkey.

teach.b: The princess chose Vishnu. Narada caught his reflection in water, and was furious, until the whole illusion faded and he saw what had happened. He'd been so full of I, I did it, that he couldn't see.
And he never forgot it. That's how the Shiva Purana tells it, and in the old pun, the word Narada asked for, hari, means both Vishnu and monkey. Here's the teaching.

Hinduism calls that I-did-it voice ahamkara, the ego: literally, the I-maker. Many teachers say it's the main thing that stands between a person and God, because it takes credit for what was never only ours.

And this is where arti comes in. At dusk, in many homes, someone holds a small plate with a lamp, or a piece of camphor, and circles the flame clockwise before the image while a bell rings and the family sings.

teach.h: CAMPHOR BURNS AND LEAVES NO ASH.
teach.b: It catches fast, burns bright, and leaves no ash behind. Not a trace. Many teachers point to that: offer yourself like camphor, burn bright for God, and leave no ego behind.
So when the flame goes round, notice who it's for. Not the person holding the plate, even on their first time, even if they're proud.
The light goes to God. Narada learned that with a monkey's face. The camphor teaches it every evening.

how: At home, many Hindus perform arti at dusk (and often at dawn) by circling a small ghee lamp or burning camphor clockwise before the image while a bell is rung and an arti song is sung; camphor, which burns away completely, is often explained as an image of offering up the ego.

o: a scented oil rubbed on the image's feet
what burns bright and leaves no ash
the ghee that soaks a lamp's cotton wick

p: a name of Vishnu, and a word for monkey
burns bright and leaves no ash

s: Vishnu gave Narada his own handsome face
he gave him a monkey's face, to cure his pride.
in Hindu teaching, ahamkara means the ego, the I-maker
the voice that says 'i did it', which many teachers call the main wall between a person and God.
camphor is used in arti partly because it leaves no ash
many teachers say: burn bright for God and leave no ego behind.

games.q: it's your first time leading arti and it goes perfectly. everyone's watching you. what fits today's teaching?
o: soak it up: you did that.
remember who the light is for, and let the credit go with the camphor.
stop doing arti so you don't get proud.
games.why: the flame goes to God, not to the one holding the plate. camphor burns and leaves no ash; many teachers say the ego should go the same way.

practice: If you have a candle or small lamp and it's safe, light it and hold it steady on a plate in your right hand; if not, use your open hand, or just your eyes. Before an image, a photo or a window, make a few slow circles clockwise.
If you pray, say a name you honor as the light goes round. Then think of one thing you're proud of this week, and offer the credit with the light. Set it down and sit with the flame.

wordCard.voice: Camphor: the arti flame that burns bright and leaves no ash, offered to God, with the ego going up along with it.

orig.note: Sanskrit karpūra: camphor. In Hindi often kapoor, burned in arti.

carryVoice: Your line: burn the ego like camphor. Narada asked for Vishnu's face, and got a monkey's. That's day one hundred nineteen.

sources.ref: Shiva Purana, Rudra Samhita, Srishti Khanda, chapters 2-4 (Narada's pride; the illusory city and swayamvara; the monkey face)
